Calibrate an LLM-as-judge against human labels

Source: R/calibrate.R
calibrate_judge.Rd

Runs a judge on a redacted view of a human-labeled set and reports agreement, confusion metrics, and (for multiple human raters) human reliability. The result is descriptive evidence; deployment decisions require an explicit acceptance_policy().

Usage

calibrate_judge(
  gold,
  judge = NULL,
  input_cols = NULL,
  id_col = NULL,
  human_cols = "human_label",
  judge_col = "judge_label",
  label_levels = NULL,
  scale = c("nominal", "ordinal"),
  weights = NULL,
  coefficients = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  n_boot = 2000,
  seed = NULL,
  provenance = list(),
  audit_id = NULL
)

Arguments

gold

A data frame of labeled examples.

judge

A function receiving the redacted judge input, or NULL to read precomputed labels from judge_col.

input_cols

Columns visible to judge. Required when judge is a function. Human columns and judge_col are forbidden.

id_col

Optional unique item identifier. A sequential internal ID is generated when omitted.

human_cols

Human-rater columns. Supplying more than one enables the modal-consensus rule described in the "Human consensus" section and the human-reliability benchmark.

judge_col

Column containing precomputed judge labels when judge is NULL.

label_levels

Complete label universe in intended order. Labels are matched exactly (case and whitespace are significant) and empty labels are rejected; represent a failed judgement as NA. Required for scale = "ordinal". When NULL, the universe is inferred from the human and judge labels together: when factor columns (or a judge returning a factor) declare at least two levels between them, those levels come first, then any other observed label; otherwise the observed labels in the order first seen. A label only the judge used is then a category, not an error; when label_levels is supplied, every human and judge label must be in it.

scale

Whether labels are nominal or ordinal.

weights

Agreement weights. NULL selects "unweighted" for nominal labels and "ordinal" for ordinal labels. Weighted coefficients use Gwet's weight schemes; see agreement().

coefficients

Passed to agreement(). NULL (the default) selects Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, and Gwet's AC1, with AC2 replacing AC1 for weighted (ordinal) runs.

conf_level, n_boot, seed

Passed to agreement().

provenance

Optional named list describing the judge model, prompt, parameters, and other audit metadata.

audit_id

Optional identifier for the frozen judge, prompt, and dataset snapshot. Use the same non-empty value for related bias and stability evidence so report() can prevent accidental cross-run bundling.

Value

A yourhonor_calibration object with agreement, confusion and per-class metrics, human reliability, judge-versus-each-rater agreement, item-level evidence, label metadata, and provenance. human_ceiling remains as a compatibility alias for human_reliability but is no longer described as an upper bound.

Item-level elements:

  • items: gold plus .item_id (source-row key), .judge_item_id (the shuffled key the judge saw; NA when judge = NULL), the judge label, agree, and for several raters human_consensus, n_human_observed, and consensus_tie.

  • judge_output: the judge's own returned rows, in the order returned by the judge, keyed by .judge_item_id with .item_id joined in and label as character; NULL when judge = NULL. The judge must not return a .judge_item_id column of its own.

  • blinding_map: one row per item mapping .judge_item_id to .item_id; NULL when judge = NULL.

Exclusion counts: n_input items were supplied, n_items had a usable human consensus and judge label, n_excluded = n_input - n_items, and n_consensus_ties and n_insufficient_human_ratings break the exclusions down for multi-rater runs.

Judge abstentions: n_judge_abstentions counts items with a human reference but no judge label, judge_abstention_rate divides it by the items with a human reference, and judge_abstention_conf_low and judge_abstention_conf_high are its Clopper-Pearson interval. See the "Missing labels and abstentions" section.

The judge contract

When judge is supplied, input_cols is required. The judge receives only a generated .item_id plus those columns; human labels and existing judge labels are never exposed. It may return either one label per input row or a data frame with .item_id and label columns. Structured output is preferred because IDs make accidental reordering detectable.

Items are shuffled before grading and the .item_id the judge sees is assigned after the shuffle, so it is not the source row number. The result keeps both keys: items$.item_id is the source-row audit key and items$.judge_item_id is the key the judge saw. Join judge-side logs (prompts, raw completions) on .judge_item_id, never on .item_id.

Human consensus

With one column in human_cols the human label is used as given. With several, each item's reference label is the modal (most frequent) human label. An item with fewer than two observed human ratings has no consensus and is counted in n_insufficient_human_ratings; an item whose most frequent labels tie has no consensus either, is flagged in items$consensus_tie, and is counted in n_consensus_ties. Items without a consensus are excluded from the judge-versus-consensus agreement and confusion evidence (n_excluded). Because ties are exactly the items humans found hardest, and with two raters every human disagreement is a tie, the judge is scored only on the items humans agreed about; that direction is optimistic. per_rater_agreement compares the judge against each rater on every item and is the all-items counterpart.

Missing labels and abstentions

Encode a judge abstention, refusal, or unparseable output as NA in the judge label (or return NA from judge); never as a sentinel label such as "abstain", which would be scored as a category. Encode a missing human rating as NA in its human column. The two are reported separately: an item with a human reference and an NA judge label is a judge abstention (n_judge_abstentions), while an item without a human reference is a gap in the gold set. Both are excluded from agreement and counted in n_excluded, which acceptance_policy()'s max_missing_rate bounds; its optional max_abstention_rate bounds the abstention interval alone, because a judge that abstains on hard items looks more accurate on the items it did answer.

Examples

gold <- tibble::tibble(
  input = paste("answer", 1:8),
  human_label = c("C", "C", "P", "I", "C", "P", "I", "C"),
  judge_label = c("C", "C", "C", "I", "C", "P", "P", "C")
)
calibrate_judge(gold, label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
                n_boot = 200, seed = 1)
#> 
#> ── yourhonor judge calibration ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 8 usable items of 8 - descriptive judge-vs-human agreement:
#> • cohen_kappa: 0.58 [0.07, 1.00] (moderate)
#> • krippendorff_alpha: 0.60 [0.05, 1.00] (moderate)
#> • gwet_ac1: 0.65 [0.25, 1.00] (substantial)
#> 2 disagreements; inspect `confusion_metrics()` before use.
#> ℹ No deployment decision is implied; call report() with a policy to assess one.
